result:
If I had to pick one, I think I'd choose dramatically improving humanity's collective ability to reason together — something like a widespread upgrade in epistemic humility and good-faith communication.

The reason I'd pick that over more direct fixes (curing diseases, ending poverty) is that it's upstream of so much else. Many of the world's persistent problems aren't unsolvable for lack of resources or knowledge — they persist because people can't agree on what's true, can't trust each other enough to coordinate, or get locked into tribal positions where being right matters less than winning. Climate change, pandemic response, political dysfunction — all of these are partly coordination failures.

If people were better at saying "I might be wrong," genuinely listening to opposing views, and updating beliefs based on evidence, I suspect a lot of other problems would start solving themselves.

That said, I hold this answer loosely. There's a real counterargument that picking something concrete — like eliminating extreme poverty — would be better, because abstract improvements to "how people think" are vague, and meanwhile actual people are suffering in ways we know how to fix.

I'm curious what you'd choose. People's answers to this often reveal interesting things about what they see as the root problem versus the symptoms.
